what: Decode of twitter.cbor (402814 bytes) into Go values: map[string]any, []any, string, uint64, int64, float64, bool, nil, []byte. 1000 copies read in turn. Arm mb: a Go binding of mbedded-cbor main 75eaab5 through cgo, one call per document; a cbor::binding writes a flat list of items, and Go builds the values from it. Arm fx: fxamacker/cbor v2.9.4, DecMode with DefaultMapType map[string]any. Arm ug: ugorji/go codec v1.3.2, CborHandle with MapType map[string]any and RawToString. A test checks with reflect.DeepEqual that all three give the same value. Time in microseconds per document.
why: The owner asked for a Go binding, measured against the best CBOR library of Go.
how: go test -c, one binary per arm, each built twice (a, b), 3 rounds alternating, -test.benchtime=0.1s -test.count=3, b.Loop, GOAMD64=v4, GLIBC_TUNABLES trim_threshold, mmap_threshold and top_pad high (only the arm mb uses malloc). The C++ part: g++ 16.2 -std=c++23 -O2 -march=x86-64-v4 -DNDEBUG.
finding: Medians, us per document: mb 1866.4 / 1943.8, fx 4073.6 / 3925.7, ug 3426.5 / 2933.6. mb takes about half the time of fx and about 60 to 65 percent of ug. Allocations per document: mb 28045, fx 31838, ug 35704; Go heap bytes: mb 1445 KiB, fx 1494 KiB, ug 1516 KiB, without the C++ list of items, which malloc holds for the call. Noise between the two binaries of one arm: mb 4 percent, fx 4 percent, ug 17 percent. A first run, where the binding put each map key in an any before it used it as a string, gave mb 2237 / 2175 us and 41390 allocations.

context.threads: 1 goroutine; the Go runtime runs its GC on more threads
